event: VXE 978 lost altitude tracking after about 1.2 hours of flight, then lost all link and crashed during lost link descent; logs show XCOMM, VTOL AP and FDR all stopped within about 2 seconds.
component: main battery or its power connection (AS150) to the avionics
failure_mode: total avionics power loss in flight (XCOMM, VTOL AP and FDR logs cut together, next XCOMM startup logged as power reset)
contributing: insulation nicks on fuse power harness 107-102189 XT30 branch (crash or vibration, not settled)
grease found inside AS150 negative terminal
altitude tracking caution before link loss

evidence.quote: Xcomm/vtol/fdr cut all around the same time. I did see that there was some altitude tracking issue but I’m not sure it was indicative of a real problem vs. just altitude tracking issues that happen sometimes.
next startup indicates 'power reset'

taking another look at this one, still dont see anything obvious. Voltages remain healthy, FWD motor seems to be responding fine to commands. Then everything stops logging at the same time. That mixed with the lost comms makes it look like a MB internal or connection problem. Need to troubleshoot the hardware

(10/16) Wasn’t able to determine any root cause with an in-fuselage power-on of the avionics box. Moved the avionics box to the IB and posted results below. So far everything seems to be functioning normally but will continue testing functionality. Expecting to be able to inspect the battery used in-flight during crash Tuesday (10/20) for signs of power failure. - Matt A.

team_view_in_comments: That mixed with the lost comms makes it look like a MB internal or connection problem.

would_settle_it.file: main battery used in crash flight
would_settle_it.what: inspect the in-flight main battery for internal failure or signs of power interruption (scheduled 2026-10-20)
whether the material in the AS150 negative terminal is contamination that could cause an intermittent contact
MCM vsm/cucs logs to confirm the MCM also lost power at the same time; battery voltage/current just before the cut

reasoning: The XCOMM, VTOL AP and FDR logs all end within about 2 seconds of each other and the next XCOMM startup reads as a power reset, which points to a total avionics power loss. Voltages were healthy right up to the cut, and bench and iron bird power-on of the avionics box found nothing wrong, so the team suspects the main battery internally or its connection. The battery has not been inspected yet, so this stays narrowed to the main power supply path.
notes: RMA-1112 intake PDF and labels have no extractable text (scans); RMA-1113 is the gimbal (EPS6508) RMA with no findings. Data upload also contained logs labeled 885, not this tail. RMA-1112 lists customer SOCOM(SUMS) while VXEP-2007 lists USAACE. Ticket description starts mid word ('o issues').

event: VXE 426 repeatedly lost all GPS satellites 3 to 5 minutes after start, went into dead reckoning, overflew the LZ on RTB and finished with an emergency glide landing.
failure_mode: receiver stops sending outputs to the autopilots; reset logic restores it briefly then it drops out again
contributing: possible RF interference or spoofing in theater (customer was spoofed about 3 weeks earlier)
intermittent long range antenna link loss during the same flight

evidence.quote: When initially started it will show anywhere between 19-25 satellites then around 3-5 minutes later it will lose all satellites and enter dead reckoning mode.

@Zachary Mann @Alexander Alan Arnold it looks like the Novatel is stopping its outputs to the autopilots.  The reset logic is able to get it to come back for a short period but then it’s dropping out again.  Was this in theater?  If so it’s plausible there is something in the received signals that is messing up the novatel.  If we have access to the bird I’d like to recommend we request the debug data from the novatel (we have to connect to it via putty and issue some commands).  If those show a fault in the receiver we can have NovAtel provide some insight into why the receiver is not outputting data.
Update 10/12/2026: Still awaiting information from Novatel

team_view_in_comments: it looks like the Novatel is stopping its outputs to the autopilots.

would_settle_it.what: receiver fault status showing whether the unit itself faulted or was disturbed by received signals
GNSS satellite count, jamming/spoofing indicators and receiver output timing around each dropout

reasoning: The flight log review shows the NovAtel receiver stops sending data to the autopilots and only returns briefly after resets, so the GPS loss is at the receiver. Whether the receiver has a hardware fault or is being upset by the RF environment is not settled; NovAtel debug data is still awaited. The dead reckoning, RTB and glide landing were the vehicle responding to that GPS loss.
notes: The quote about the dropout was quoted with a trailing space in the description. Attachment list includes AAR_V918_B30N_20261009T171329Z.zip, which is the VXEP-2019 (tail 918) AAR, probably attached by mistake.

event: After the 6.7.1 firmware upgrade and an XCOMM update, VXE 967 could not be connected in SUAV or OGCS on the ground; the aircraft was returned and the XCOMM was found in a bootloop.
failure_mode: XCOMM stuck in a bootloop after the firmware update while the VTOL AP stayed active, so GCS could not reach the aircraft
contributing: why the update left the XCOMM in a bootloop was not found; 5 upgrade/downgrade cycles did not reproduce it

evidence.quote: @Alexander Alan Arnold i invoked the bootloader and was able to get the xcomm online. then i was able to connect to suav. i updated the xcomm to 4.72 on my suav running 6.5.
- Examine logs for what aircraft was doing/how got into state. Appears there was a bootloop state of the xcomm where it was not operating but the vtol was active.
- Upgrade downgrade many times: Performed 5 cycles due to time on 10/9/2026 and no issues seen
@Alexander Alan Arnold  yes and that bootloop is what prevented connection to the aircraft through GCS.
XCOMM software fail following the update to ASA 6.7.1, Center wing software condition unknown as connection can not be established

team_view_in_comments: yes and that bootloop is what prevented connection to the aircraft through GCS.

would_settle_it.what: full Confluence report on why the XCOMM entered the bootloop during the update

reasoning: The logs show the XCOMM in a bootloop while the VTOL AP was running, which explains why .3 and .10 answered but SUAV and OGCS could not connect. Invoking the bootloader brought the XCOMM back and later updates went through normally, and the team states the bootloop is what blocked the connection. Why the update put the XCOMM into that state was not reproduced.
notes: RMA-1114 intake PDF has no extractable text. Drew Hildreth notes the customer info on the RMA was wrong. VXEP-2015 is a similar 6.7.1 upgrade problem on a different tail (635) with a different component (center wing). Review change: agrees_with_team was yes, scored against the engineers' view in comments; set to no_team_answer because the ticket has no Root Cause field.

event: VXE 401 (with the AV box from 398) descended from 1,500 ft and, after a level up command, pitched nose down and hit the ground about 400 m from the GCS.
component: elevator (control surface or its drive on the crashed tail)
failure_mode: vehicle could not pitch up; elevator found sticking and hard to move after the crash
contributing: full standard hood payload and radio payloads (GTOW 47.8, CG reported good)

evidence.quote: @Alexander Alan Arnold @Everett Werner initial look suggests an issue with pitch control.  The vehicle tried to pitch up but couldn’t.  I think the top items to check in this case would be:

@Eric Brewer CG was good our gtow was 47.8, elevator was definitely sticking and hard to move when we recovered it but we put on it another tail and did like 50 surface checks on it and couldn’t get it to bind at all it moved normally-from customer
@Alexander Alan Arnold Got it - a sticking elevator would certainly explain what we saw - but I’d like to understand why that’s happening.

team_view_in_comments: a sticking elevator would certainly explain what we saw - but I’d like to understand why that’s happening.

would_settle_it.what: pitch command versus pitch response and elevator command/position before impact
test the elevator on the crashed tail boom to find where it binds (hinge, linkage, servo) and whether it is crash damage

reasoning: Log review shows the vehicle commanding pitch up but not achieving it, and CG and airspeed did not suggest a stall or loading problem. The elevator was found sticking after the crash but moved freely when fitted to another tail boom, so the bind may be in the crashed boom or may be crash damage. This narrows the fault to pitch control at the elevator without naming the part.

event: VXE 918 at 3000 ft AGL, 22 km out, showed a VTOL GPS error with 0 VTOL satellites, then lost comms in a steep descending left bank and crashed.
failure_mode: INS likely reported erroneous altitude and vertical speed; VTOL GPS showed 0 satellites before link loss
contributing: interference noted on 902 on the Silvus page

evidence.quote: Right now, my best guess is that the INS was reporting an erroneous altitude and vertical speed.  That would be most likely caused by a Novatel IMU failure (we have not seen one of those previously so an unlikely event) or spoofing (unless someone was running a CUAS system domestically this would be surprising?).  The logs cut off before I can get more insight into how exactly it crashed but this is what I know so far.

VXE was on way back from furthest point 53 min into flight, and was going to take apx 45 mins to RTB and still had 70% battery, PIC commanded dash to see new apx rtb time and see power draw. After commanding Cruise and adjusting route to have VXE fly closer to road looked at Silvus page to see the interference on 902, OGCS alerted to a VTOL GPS error, looked at the GNSS Tab and saw 28 for FW and 0 Sats for VTOL followed by a lost coms. Looking at the Aircraft last known location VXE 918 was in a 7620 FPM decent and at 2700 AGL 41.4 MPH IAS and in a bank to the left.
@Eric Brewer equipment requested and RMA generated, awaiting return to aid in investigation.

team_view_in_comments: Right now, my best guess is that the INS was reporting an erroneous altitude and vertical speed.

would_settle_it.what: Eric Brewer's plots of INS altitude and vertical speed against other sources
bench test of the NovAtel IMU/receiver for failure
VTOL GNSS satellite count, spoofing indicators and INS vertical channel before log cut

reasoning: The operator saw a VTOL GPS error with 0 satellites on the VTOL side while the FW side had 28, then lost comms with the vehicle in a fast descent. The engineering best guess is that the INS gave erroneous altitude and vertical speed, from either a NovAtel IMU failure or spoofing. The logs cut off and the hardware has not been returned, so this stays at the navigation system level with low confidence.
notes: RMA for the hardware was generated but no RMA key is given in the ticket. Nose cone found 350 ft from the wreck, which the team found surprising.

event: On VXE 1020 and 1068 the Ping200 transponder reported altitudes 100 to 300 ft low above 6,000 ft MSL compared with the tower and OGCS; no flight incident.
failure_mode: Ping200 reported altitude reads low by up to 300 ft at 9,000 ft MSL
contributing: possible static pressure error from transponder location in hood payload near forward motor airflow
possible confusion between pressure altitude and other altitudes shown in GCS

evidence.quote: reporting 6900ft, 8000ft was reporting 7800ft, and at 9000ft it was reporting 8700ft."
It is highly unlikely that these units (the ping hardware itself) are defective or providing incorrect information. They are TSOd hardware.
- inaccurate pressure altitude due to location of transponder (hood payload impacted by forward motor air pressure) and ping enclosed in secondary enclosure surrounding it.
in excess of ±125 feet, then calibration as described in Section  9.5

would_settle_it.what: Baro Altitude Source setting (internal or external) and other configuration
which altitudes OGCS showed and how they compare with Ping pressure altitude
ADS-B reported pressure altitude for the ICAO address used on those flights
air data test set check of the altitude encoder against the +/-125 ft limit

reasoning: The operators report the Ping200 altitude reading 100 to 300 ft low above 6,000 ft, which is outside the manual's 125 ft correspondence limit. The vendor-hardware expert doubts a unit defect and lists measurement confusion, VXE baro issues and static pressure error from the installation as more likely. No data, configuration or bench test settles which, so the cause is not determined.
notes: Two aircraft (1020 and 1068) on one ticket with the same symptom. The manual attached is for the ping200XR, while the comment says RDW uses the Ping200X. The dust cover on the static port was checked and not installed.

event: On RTB, VXE 853 climbed to about 8,700 ft AGL and would not descend for over an hour until operators flew long racetracks and recovered it safely.
failure_mode: vehicle held in a strong updraft climbed several thousand feet with throttle nearly off; airframe drag too low to descend
contributing: limited drag/descent capability of the airframe at idle
reported loss of link not analyzed

evidence.quote: @Alexander Alan Arnold @Scott Whitney @David Grosher pretty wild, I’ve never seen this but it looks like it must have been hanging out in an updraft.  All the altitude estimates (GPS/Baro) agree that the vehicle was climbing, and it barely touched the throttle.  This plot below is almost a full hour and it barely touched the throttle but still climbed several thousand feet even at dash speeds.  Current draw agrees that front prop and vtol motors were not on during this time.  Nothing wrong with the airplane as far as I can tell, we just don’t make enough drag to descend in these conditions.

Currently, the VXE30 Stalker System is quarantined until the issue is identified. The USMC Fleet unit launched a different AV tail number and performed a RTB test to determine whether the issue persisted, and it did not. The new AV tail number executed the RTB flawlessly.

team_view_in_comments: it looks like it must have been hanging out in an updraft.

would_settle_it.what: altitude, throttle and current over the hour showing climb with motors off

reasoning: The log review shows GPS and baro altitude agreeing that the vehicle climbed while throttle was barely used and current draw showed the front prop and VTOL motors off. That rules out a sensor or pitot fault giving false altitude and points to strong rising air the airframe could not out-descend. The operators' other ideas (pitot, overheated avionics) are not supported by the data.
notes: Alexander Alan Arnold also mentions loss of link and uncommanded climbs; the link loss with legacy GCS was referred to Craig Burton and Ted Trowbridge with no answer in the ticket.
